fields.sample_size: 26 interviews (municipalities 3, national 1 and provincial 1 water and sanitation departments, civic organisations 5, community leaders 5, advocacy groups 5, researchers 3, entrepreneurs 3) plus a 60-minute focus group with resident lobby groups, in three Western Cape municipal jurisdictions; purposive sampling to saturation; documentary review; content analysis (interviews about 40 minutes)
fields.effect_estimate: Interviewees credit the Free Basic Sanitation (FBSan) policy with reducing backlogs but identify a disconnection between policy and practice: subjective clauses read differently by consumers and municipalities; no norms or standards for service levels, facility types or who qualifies; municipalities have wide latitude on technology and service level; no enforcement or accountability mechanism for consumer participation; fragmented institutional roles across national, provincial and local government and across municipal units; political promises and interference triggering violent protests; skills shortages and political appointments; difficult land conditions. Stakeholders propose clarifying policy clauses, norms and standards, accountability and monitoring, skills-based appointments, consumer engagement and depoliticisation (Table 1). Qualitative; interviews analysed as a whole, not by sector.
fields.study_design: qualitative study (interviews, focus group and document review; three municipalities, Western Cape)
fields.section: Full text: Materials and methods (26 interviews, focus group, content analysis); Results and discussion (challenges, proposed solutions, Table 1); Conclusion
fields.exact_location: Materials and methods (26 interviews, focus group, content analysis); Results and discussion (challenges, proposed solutions, Table 1); Conclusion

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: 26 stakeholder interviews and a focus group on Free Basic Sanitation policy in three Western Cape municipalities, read in full text 2026-10-04. Subjective policy clauses, no norms and standards, no enforcement or accountability, fragmented institutions and political interference explain the policy-practice gap.
